verses.note: Joseph's faithfulness is a matter of repeated refusal over time, not a single heroic act. Scripture's counsel about sexual temptation follows the same line: keep distance from it and flee (Proverbs 5:8, 2 Timothy 2:22).
Wholeness before God is defined here as undivided trust. Israel's integrity consists not in moral perfection but in refusing to seek guidance or security from any source God has forbidden.
Stability comes from attention. The psalmist is unshaken not because nothing threatens him but because he keeps God before him, a discipline as much as a feeling.

Paul takes up this image and the related one of 59:17 for believers: stand firm with the belt of truth around your waist and the breastplate of righteousness (Ephesians 6:14). The king's own equipment becomes the armor of those who belong to him.

The Spirit's work does not replace obedience; it produces it. Paul's teaching that the law's requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit (Romans 8:4) and his call to walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16) stand on this verse's logic. How divine enabling and human action relate is debated between Augustinian, Reformed, Wesleyan, and other traditions, but all hold both.

The desire for righteousness is itself blessed, and the filling is God's work. The verse keeps together a longing for a right life and the promise that God will satisfy it, which is why it has served both as a comfort to the guilty and a spur to the complacent.

Holiness requires decisive action against whatever leads to sin, even when it costs something precious. The warning is grounded in the reality of final judgment, which Jesus treats as serious enough to justify any loss.

Christians have understood the command in different ways: the medieval distinction between precepts for all and counsels of perfection for some; Luther's view that it exposes the need for grace; John Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection (A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, 1766) as wholehearted love made possible by grace; and the common view that it names the goal of maturity toward which disciples grow.

The healed woman rises and serves, and the verb is diakoneō, the word Jesus uses for his own mission (20:28). Matthew's compression makes her the first person in his Gospel whose restoration issues at once in service to Jesus, the pattern of a life that is healed in order to serve.

Jesus does not remove obedience but changes its character. The life he calls disciples to is still a yoke, yet it is borne with him and under a kind master, which is why 1 John 5:3 can say that God's commands are not burdensome.

The Christian life is shaped by the shape of Christ's own life. Self-denial here is not self-hatred but the surrender of the self's claim to rule, and the cross is not ordinary hardship but the loss that comes from following Jesus. The chapter note's pastoral warning applies: this verse never requires anyone to submit to abuse.

Holiness in this saying is ruthless toward one's own sin, not toward others. The images are deliberately extreme to show that no habit, relationship, or practice is worth keeping if it leads to ruin. Anyone struggling with thoughts of self-harm should hear clearly that Jesus is speaking in figures, and should seek help from someone they trust.

The garment has been read as works of righteousness (Irenaeus), as charity (Augustine, Gregory the Great), as the righteousness of Christ given to the believer, and as the fruit of repentance. Calvin refused to separate faith from a holy life here. What the story itself requires is that the one who accepts the king's invitation comes changed by it, and the man's silence shows he knew it. Revelation 19:8 describes the bride's fine linen as the righteous acts of the saints, given to her to wear.
The saying about willing spirit and weak flesh names the gap between good intention and actual strength that every disciple knows. Jesus does not excuse the gap; he tells them to pray because of it.

The disciples are to keep in themselves the salt that makes them useful and to live at peace with one another. After an argument about rank, Jesus names peace among his followers as a mark of the life the fire refines.

The contrast of willing spirit and weak flesh does not excuse failure; it explains why prayer is necessary. Readiness of heart does not carry a person through trial without dependence on God, which is what Jesus himself models in the same scene.
The Christian life is described as a daily self-denial and a continuing following. Holiness in Luke's terms is not an achievement but the pattern of a life that keeps choosing Jesus over itself.

Moral cleanup without the presence of God is not safety. The house must be occupied, and in Luke's larger story the gift that fills it is the Holy Spirit whom the Father gives to those who ask (verse 13).

A disciple's worth lies in being distinctively what Christ has made him, as salt's worth lies in its saltiness. The saying warns that a following which loses its distinctive character, its loyalty to Jesus above family, life, and possessions, has lost its usefulness, and it leaves the hearer with a call to listen rather than a formula for restoration.
The verse describes the shape of discipleship: life is kept by being given up. Clinging to one's life, like Lot's wife clinging to what she left, is the way to lose it.

Watchfulness in Luke is not scanning the news for signs but guarding the heart against what dulls it. The two named dangers are opposites, indulgence and worry, and both are the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the sower (8:14).
The washing Jesus insists on pictures the cleansing that comes from him alone, which later New Testament writers connect with his death (1 John 1:7) and with the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5).

Many interpreters since Augustine have read the bath as the decisive cleansing believers receive in Christ and the foot washing as the ongoing cleansing from the sins of daily life (1 John 1:9). Others, especially those who follow the shorter text without ‘except the feet’, read one complete cleansing. Either reading holds that the clean are made clean by Jesus, not by themselves.

The Father's care for fruitful branches is to cut them back so that they bear more. The verse presents growth in holiness as the Father's work on those already joined to the vine, a work that can include loss, and verse 3 names the word of Jesus as its chief instrument.

Holiness is not withdrawal. Jesus explicitly declines to pray that his people be removed from the world; he prays that they be guarded within it. The verse has been a check both on flight from ordinary life and on its opposite, a church indistinguishable from the world around it.

The means of sanctification is God's word. The disciples are set apart not by leaving the world but by being claimed by the truth, the word Jesus has given them. The same connection appears in 15:3, where they are clean because of the word he has spoken.
The chain describes growth in holiness through testing. Character is formed under pressure, and the believer's endurance is itself evidence of God's work.

‘Walk in newness of life’ names the goal of union with Christ in ordinary behavior. Holiness is not an addition to the gospel but its purpose: the believer dies with Christ so that he can live a different life.

Holiness begins from something God has done, not something believers achieve: the old self ‘was crucified’. Reformed and Lutheran readers stress that this is a change of dominion with sin still present; Wesleyan readers take it as the basis for a real and growing freedom from willful sin. Both read the verse as the ground of the commands that follow.

The command not to let sin reign shows that its power is broken but its pressure is not gone. Sanctification is the believer, freed from sin's dominion, actively and repeatedly handing himself to God.

Hagiasmos, holiness or sanctification, appears here and in verse 22 as the direction of the new life. Paul presents it as a road with a destination: slavery to righteousness leads to holiness, as slavery to impurity led to more lawlessness.

Walking by the Spirit is the shape of Christian obedience. The verse joins justification (verse 3) and sanctification (verse 4) without merging them: God's sentence on sin in Christ has as its purpose a life that fulfills his law.

Putting sin to death is done ‘by the Spirit’ and by the believer at once. The Puritan John Owen built his treatise Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656) on this verse, arguing that the work is the believer's duty and the Spirit's power together.

Paul connects belief about the body's future with conduct in the body now, as he did in 6:13-14. Denial of the resurrection is not treated as a harmless opinion; it loosens moral seriousness because it empties the body of lasting significance.

The Christian life continues as it began. The Spirit who started the work is the one who completes it (Philippians 1:6), and growth does not switch to a different power source once a person is converted.

Good works are neither the root of salvation nor an optional extra. God created the new life for them and prepared them in advance, so a life of good works is the expected shape of salvation, the evidence of God's workmanship.

Christian growth is described as taking on a mind, a way of thinking and valuing, that belongs to Christ. The ethical reading and the salvation-story reading are not finally opposed: those who are in Christ are to think in the way his story reveals.
Holiness is neither passive nor self-generated. The believer truly wills and acts, and God is truly the one who works in that willing and acting.
Knowledge of God and a changed life belong together in both directions: knowledge leads to fruit, and fruitful living deepens knowledge. The Christian life is pictured as growth, not a fixed state.
The goal of reconciliation is a people presented holy and blameless before God. Holiness is both the result of Christ's work and the condition in which God intends to present his people.
The goal of ministry is maturity for every believer, reached by teaching and admonition centered on Christ. No inner circle holds a higher perfection.
Holiness is given by Jesus to those who belong to him. The verse makes sanctification both his work and the basis of a family bond: the Holy One and the made-holy belong together.
Spiritual understanding can decline. The readers had once heard well (2:3) and had become dull, which is why the letter treats hearing God's word as something to be guarded (3:7, 4:7).
Growth takes practice over time. The perfect participle pictures faculties that have been exercised and now stand ready, which is the goal of the teaching Hebrews wants to give.

The old rites could make the body ritually clean but could not reach the conscience. The verse locates the human problem in the conscience, the inner awareness of guilt before God, which only Christ's blood reaches (verse 14).

Believers ‘have been sanctified’ by Christ's offering: consecrated to God once and for all, the sense the Reformed theologian John Murray called definitive sanctification. Hebrews also speaks of the ongoing pursuit of holiness (12:14); the two belong together, the first as the ground of the second.

A completed perfection and an ongoing sanctification stand side by side. Believers' standing before God is settled by Christ's offering, while their growth in holiness continues, and the first secures the second.
